story: Nüwa, a mother goddess, created humanity out of loneliness. She molded people from yellow clay by hand, and these became the wealthy and noble. Because shaping each person individually was exhausting, she dragged a string through mud to mass-produce the rest of humanity, who became the commoners. A great battle between deities broke the pillars that held up the sky, causing heaven to collapse partly, fires to rage uncontrollably, floods that would not recede, and fierce beasts to attack ordinary people. Nüwa smelted five-colored stones to patch the holes in the sky, cut the legs off a giant turtle to serve as new pillars, killed a black dragon blamed for the flooding, and piled up reeds and ashes to stop the surging waters. Order was restored: the sky was mended, the pillars stood firm, the waters drained, and people were safe. Nüwa was the sister, and later wife, of Fuxi. Before marrying, the two lived on a sacred mountain; ashamed of their feelings for each other, they prayed that if heaven approved their marriage, mist would gather over the mountain. The mist gathered, confirming their union. When they became intimate, they made a fan from grass to hide their faces, which is said to be why fans are used in marriage customs today. In another version, after surviving a great flood, the pair married by heaven's command, and Nüwa gave birth to a ball of flesh, which was cut into pieces that scattered across the world and became human beings. In a later legend, Nüwa was honored for having mended the heavens long ago. A king who saw her temple statue lusted after her image and wrote a lewd poem on a nearby wall. Enraged, Nüwa vowed that his dynasty would fall as punishment, and she sent three spirit subordinates to bewitch him, contributing to the eventual collapse of his rule.
